title: C & C++
blurb: Memory, pointers, UB, RAII, templates and modern C++.

quiz.question: What happens when you dereference a pointer after free() in C?
quiz.explanation: Use-after-free is undefined behaviour and a major source of security bugs. Set pointers to NULL after free and use tools like AddressSanitizer.

quiz.question: RAII in C++ means…
options: Resources are acquired in constructors and released in destructors, tied to object lifetime
quiz.explanation: RAII makes cleanup automatic and exception-safe: std::unique_ptr, std::lock_guard and std::fstream all release their resources when they go out of scope.

quiz.question: Which smart pointer expresses exclusive ownership?
quiz.explanation: unique_ptr is move-only with zero overhead; shared_ptr uses reference counting; weak_ptr observes without owning; auto_ptr was removed in C++17.

quiz.question: What does std::move actually do?
options: Casts its argument to an rvalue reference so a move constructor or move assignment can be chosen
quiz.explanation: std::move is just a cast; the move happens only if a move operation is selected. The moved-from object stays valid but in an unspecified state.

quiz.question: Why is a virtual destructor needed in a polymorphic base class?
options: So deleting a derived object through a base pointer calls the derived destructor
quiz.explanation: Without it, delete base_ptr is undefined behaviour and typically skips the derived destructor, leaking resources.

problems.title: Find the bugs
problems.prompt: char *dup(const char *s) { char *d = malloc(strlen(s)); strcpy(d, s); return d; } — find and fix the bugs.
problems.solution: It allocates one byte too few (no room for the '\0'), so strcpy overflows, and it doesn't check malloc's result. Fix: size_t n = strlen(s) + 1; char *d = malloc(n); if (!d) return NULL; memcpy(d, s, n); return d; (or use strdup, standard since C23).

problems.title: Rule of zero
problems.prompt: A class owns a heap buffer via a raw pointer and has a hand-written destructor but no copy constructor. What goes wrong, and what's the modern fix?
problems.solution: Copying the object copies the pointer, so both copies free the same buffer (double free) — the rule of three/five was violated. Modern fix (rule of zero): hold the buffer in std::vector or std::unique_ptr<T[]>, delete the hand-written destructor, and let the compiler-generated operations do the right thing.
